title: The DOM: Selecting, Changing and Listening
sub: Treat a page as a live tree of objects you can query, rewrite and wire to events, without opening an XSS hole
goals: Walk the node tree and pick elements with getElementById, querySelector(All), closest and matches
Change text, attributes, classes and styles, and explain why textContent beats innerHTML for untrusted data
Build and insert elements in batches with createElement, append, DocumentFragment and template cloning
Handle events with options, propagation and delegation, including a form that POSTs to an API
Render lists from fetched data with loading, empty and error states, polling and debounced search
Persist small UI state in localStorage and react to changes with MutationObserver and IntersectionObserver

blocks.text: In this chapter you will stop treating HTML as text and start treating it as a data structure. The browser turns every page into a tree of objects, the DOM, and JavaScript can find any node in that tree, change it, create new ones and react when the user clicks or types. You will build the pieces of a live device dashboard against the practice server at `lab.local`: a filterable list rendered from `/api/devices`, a form that POSTs a new device and shows the API's validation errors, a status line that polls `/api/status`, and a search box that does not flood the server. Along the way you will break a page with an injected `` and fix it, which is the single most important security lesson of front-end work.

Every `webplay` below has a DevTools drawer: watch the tree change in **Elements**, poke at the page in **Console**. On any real page: Chrome ⌥⌘J (Console) or ⌥⌘C (inspect an element); Safari ⌥⌘C once developer features are switched on (see [Browser DevTools](#devtools)).
The tree the browser builds

When HTML arrives, the parser does not keep the text. It tokenizes the bytes and builds a tree of objects in memory: the **Document Object Model**. The DOM is an API defined by the WHATWG *DOM Standard* and *HTML Standard*, a set of interfaces (`Node`, `Element`, `HTMLElement`, `Text`, `Document`, `Event`) that every engine implements. Blink (Chrome), WebKit (Safari) and Gecko (Firefox) store the tree in C++; JavaScript gets wrapper objects that read and write it. Change a wrapper and the engine schedules a re-render. The source you see with ⌥⌘U never changes; the Elements panel shows the live tree.

blocks.text: `nodeValue` is `null` for elements; text and comments carry their characters there. Most of the time you want the element-only properties, because whitespace nodes are noise:
window and document

Two globals start every DOM script. `window` is the **global object** of the page: `setTimeout`, `fetch`, `localStorage`, `location`, `history`, `innerWidth` and every global variable live on it, so `window.fetch === fetch`. `document` is the root of the tree (`window.document`), with `document.documentElement` (`<html>`), `document.head` and `document.body` as shortcuts.

blocks.title: Elements with an id leak into the global scope

blocks.text: The HTML standard says every element with an `id` is also reachable as a property of `window` ("named access"). On the page above, typing `clients` in the console returns the `<ul>`. Never rely on it: any global variable with the same name wins, and names like `status` or `name` already exist on `window`. Use `document.getElementById('clients')`.

blocks.name: element.children
blocks.sum: The element children of a node as a live HTMLCollection; childNodes includes text and comment nodes too.

how.text: `children` returns an `HTMLCollection` of the child **elements** in document order, skipping the whitespace text nodes and comments that `childNodes` includes. Both collections are **live**: they are views onto the tree, so adding or removing a child changes them immediately.

An `HTMLCollection` has `length`, index access and `item()`, but no `forEach`, `map` or `filter`. Spread it (`[...el.children]`) or use `Array.from()` to get a real array. `childNodes` is a `NodeList`, which does have `forEach`.

blocks.text: Selecting elements

Every DOM task starts by getting a reference to the right node. There are two families: the CSS-selector methods (`querySelector`, `querySelectorAll`, `closest`, `matches`), which accept any selector you learned in [CSS](#css), and the older direct lookups (`getElementById`, `getElementsByClassName`, `getElementsByTagName`).

blocks.name: document.getElementById()
blocks.sum: Return the element whose id attribute matches, or null.

how.text: The fastest lookup there is: engines keep a hash map from id to element, so the cost does not grow with page size. The argument is the bare id, **without** `#`. Ids should be unique; if a page breaks that rule, you get the first one in document order.

blocks.name: element.querySelector()
blocks.sum: Return the first descendant that matches a CSS selector, or null.

how.text: The engine walks the subtree in document order and returns the first element matching the selector list. Any selector works: ids, classes, attributes (`[data-ip^="192.168."]`), combinators and pseudo-classes such as `:checked`, `:not()`, `:has()`. Called on `document` it searches the whole page; called on an element it searches only below that element, which is faster and avoids matching the wrong copy of a repeated widget.
An invalid selector throws a `SyntaxError` (a `DOMException`), so a typo fails loudly. Pseudo-elements like `::before` never match because they are not nodes.

blocks.name: element.querySelectorAll()
blocks.sum: Return every descendant matching a CSS selector as a static NodeList.

how.text: Returns all matches in document order as a **static** `NodeList`: a snapshot that does not update when the tree changes, which makes it safe to loop over while you modify elements. When nothing matches you get an empty list, not `null`, so `.length` and `forEach` are always safe.
A `NodeList` has `forEach`, `entries`, `keys` and `values`, but not `map`, `filter` or `reduce`. Spread it into an array (`[...list]`) or use `Array.from(list, fn)` to chain array methods.

blocks.name: element.closest()
blocks.sum: Walk up from an element (starting with itself) and return the first ancestor that matches a selector.

how.text: `closest` tests the element itself, then its parent, grandparent and so on up to `<html>`, and returns the first match or `null`. It is the workhorse of **event delegation**: the click target may be a `<b>` or an icon deep inside a row, and `e.target.closest('tr')` climbs to the row that holds the data.
Because it includes the starting element, `li.closest('li')` returns `li` itself.

XSS: when text becomes code

**Cross-site scripting** (XSS) happens when data an attacker controls is parsed as markup in your page. The injected code runs with your page's full privileges: it can read cookies that are not `HttpOnly`, read tokens in `localStorage`, call your APIs as the logged-in user, and rewrite the page. The classic route is `innerHTML` plus a string that came from a form, a URL, an API or another user.

Put untrusted data into the page with `textContent`, `createElement` plus `append`, or `setAttribute` for ordinary attributes. Treat `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, `eval`, `new Function` and string arguments to `setTimeout` as **sinks** that must only ever see trusted strings.
"Untrusted" includes form fields, `location.search` and `location.hash`, API responses, `localStorage`, `postMessage` data and anything another user typed.
URL attributes are a sink too: `a.href = userUrl` with `javascript:alert(1)` runs code on click. Check the scheme with `new URL(userUrl, location.href).protocol` against `http:` and `https:`.

When you must render user-supplied HTML (a comment with formatting), sanitize it: the long-standing library is DOMPurify; the built-in `element.setHTML()` from the HTML Sanitizer API shipped in Firefox 148 and Chrome and Edge 146 in 2026, but Safari 27.2 (November 2026) does not have it yet, so keep DOMPurify for pages that must work in Safari.

Defence in depth on the server: a `Content-Security-Policy` header such as `script-src 'self'` blocks inline handlers like `onerror` even when an injection slips through, and `HttpOnly` cookies cannot be read by script at all.

blocks.name: node.textContent
blocks.sum: Get all the text inside a node, or replace its children with one text node.

how.text: Reading concatenates the data of every descendant text node in document order, ignoring CSS, so hidden elements and the contents of `<script>` and `<style>` are included and line breaks are whatever whitespace the source had. It never triggers layout.

Writing removes every child and inserts a single `Text` node holding the string verbatim. The string is never parsed, so `<`, `>` and `&` stay literal characters. That makes it the default, safe way to show data you did not write yourself. `el.textContent = ''` is also a quick way to empty an element.

blocks.text: Attributes, properties, classes and styles

An **attribute** is part of the markup: a name and a string value stored on the element (`<input value="192.168.1.50">`). A **property** is a field on the JavaScript object. Many properties *reflect* an attribute (`el.id` reads and writes the `id` attribute), but the important ones for forms do not: the `value` attribute is the *default* value, while the `value` property is the *current* value the user typed.

items.text: Typing (or assigning) changed the `value` **property**; the attribute still holds the original, which is what `form.reset()` restores. `defaultValue` is the property that reflects the attribute.
`checked` behaves the same way: the property is the live state, the attribute is the initial state.
`a.href` is the **resolved, absolute** URL (resolved against `<base>` or the page URL); `getAttribute('href')` is the string exactly as written.

`data-*` attributes appear on `dataset` with the `data-` prefix removed and kebab-case turned into camelCase (`data-device-id` → `deviceId`). Every value is a **string**, so `'false'` is truthy. Compare with `=== 'true'`, or convert with `Number()`.
A few names differ between the two worlds because they are JavaScript keywords: the `class` attribute is `className`, `for` on a label is `htmlFor`.

blocks.text: Classes beat inline styles

To change how something looks, toggle a **class** and let CSS decide what the class means. `classList` gives you `add`, `remove`, `toggle(name, force)`, `contains` and `replace`. Keep the `style` property for values that are computed at run time (a progress bar width, a position, a CSS custom property). Inline styles win most cascade fights, so scattering them makes the stylesheet impossible to reason about; classes keep presentation in CSS, work with transitions and media queries, and are easy to find in DevTools.

A third option is often the cleanest: put the **state** in a `data-*` attribute and select on it in CSS (`[data-state="offline"] .badge`). The data, the styling hook and what the Elements pane shows are then the same thing.

blocks.name: element.getAttribute()
blocks.sum: Read an attribute's string value as written in the markup; setAttribute, removeAttribute, hasAttribute and toggleAttribute change it.

how.text: Attributes are name/value string pairs stored on the element. `getAttribute` returns the exact string (or `null` if absent); `setAttribute` converts the value to a string and stores it. blocks.text: Inserting a node that is already in the tree **moves** it; a node has exactly one parent. Clone it if you want two.
Batches: DocumentFragment and template

Each insertion into a live document may invalidate style and layout. Appending 500 rows one by one is usually fine in modern engines because layout runs lazily, but reading a layout value in between (see [Performance](#perf)) makes it slow. A `DocumentFragment` is a lightweight, parentless container: build the rows inside it, then insert the fragment once. Appending a fragment moves its children and leaves it empty.

A `<template>` element holds inert markup: it is parsed but not rendered, its images do not load, and its scripts do not run. Its `.content` is a `DocumentFragment` you clone for each record. This keeps the markup in HTML, where it belongs, and the data in JavaScript.

blocks.name: document.createElement()
blocks.sum: Create a new, detached element with the given tag name.

how.text: Returns an element that belongs to the document but is not in the tree yet, so nothing renders until you insert it. Set its text with `textContent`, attributes with `setAttribute` or properties, then attach it with `append`, `before` and friends. In an HTML document the tag name is lower-cased and the element is in the HTML namespace.

blocks.name: element.append()
blocks.sum: Insert nodes or strings after the last child of an element (prepend inserts before the first).

how.text: Accepts any number of `Node`s and strings; strings become `Text` nodes, never HTML, so `append(userInput)` is XSS-safe. A node that is already in the document is **moved**, not copied. A `DocumentFragment` argument inserts its children and leaves the fragment empty.

blocks.name: element.before()
blocks.sum: Insert nodes or strings just before (or with after(), just after) an element, as its siblings.

how.text: Places the new nodes immediately before or after `el` in its parent. It works like `append` (strings become text, existing nodes move) and replaces the old `parent.insertBefore(node, el.nextSibling)` dance.

blocks.name: element.remove()
blocks.sum: Detach an element from the tree; replaceWith() swaps it for other nodes and replaceChildren() empties or refills a parent.

how.text: `remove()` takes the element out of its parent. The object still exists while you hold a reference, so you can insert it elsewhere later. Its event listeners are garbage-collected with it once nothing points at it. `replaceWith` removes the element and inserts the given nodes in its place in one step.

`replaceChildren()` with no arguments removes every child, the clean way to clear a list before re-rendering; with arguments it clears and appends in one operation, so the user never sees an empty intermediate state.

blocks.name: element.insertAdjacentHTML()
blocks.sum: Parse an HTML string and insert the nodes at one of four positions relative to an element.

how.text: Parses the string as HTML in the context of the element and inserts the result without touching existing children, so it is faster than `innerHTML +=` and keeps listeners on the old nodes. The positions are named after the element's tags: `beforebegin` (before the opening tag, a sibling), `afterbegin` (first child), `beforeend` (last child), `afterend` (after the closing tag, a sibling).
The companions `insertAdjacentElement(pos, el)` and `insertAdjacentText(pos, text)` insert a node or plain text at the same positions without parsing.

blocks.name: document.createDocumentFragment()
blocks.sum: Create an empty, parentless container to build many nodes before inserting them in one operation.

how.text: A fragment is a minimal document-like node with no parent and no rendering. Nodes appended to it do not touch the live page, so building a big list inside it costs no style or layout work. When you append the fragment to the document, its children move into the tree in one operation and the fragment becomes empty, ready for reuse.

blocks.sum: Deep-copy the inert markup inside a template element so you can fill it with data and insert it.

how.text: The `<template>` element's children are parsed into a separate `DocumentFragment` (`.content`) owned by an inert document: nothing renders, images do not load, scripts do not run, and `template.children` is empty. Each `cloneNode(true)` gives you a fresh deep copy of that fragment. blocks.text: Events in depth

The browser fires an **event** object whenever something happens: a click, a key press, a form submission, a network-driven image load, the document finishing parsing. Your code subscribes with `addEventListener`, and the browser calls your function from the event loop when the event occurs (see [the event loop](#js-deeper) for the queueing rules).

tokens.exp: the target: any Node, window or document
the event type, a string without the "on" prefix
{...}, => the listener; it receives the Event object

tokens.tok: { once: true, passive: true, capture: false, signal }

Effect
Typical use

promise not to call `preventDefault()`, so the browser can scroll without waiting
the listener is removed when the `AbortController` aborts

`true` for real user actions, `false` for events your code dispatched

The button's listener called `preventDefault()`, which cancelled the button's default action, submitting the form. The listener had `once: true`, so on the second click it was gone, nothing cancelled the default, and the form's `submit` event fired. Without the `preventDefault()` in that submit listener, the browser would have navigated away (in your own pages, a full reload).
Propagation: capture, target, bubble

blocks.code:
⟪c:1. CAPTURE⟫ (down)                         ⟪m:3. BUBBLE⟫ (up)
   window ─────────────┐                          ┌──────────── window
   document ───────────┤                          ├──────────── document
   <body> ─────────────┤                          ├──────────── <body>
   <section#panel> ────┤                          ├──── <section#panel>   ◀ stopPropagation() here
   <div.card> ─────────┤                          ├──────── <div.card>       stops the rest

                  listeners on the target run in registration order

blocks.text: Every event dispatched into the tree takes this path. Capture listeners run on the way down from `window`; then the target's own listeners; then, **if the event bubbles**, bubble listeners from the parent up to `window`. Most events bubble: `click`, `input`, `change`, `submit`, `keydown`. Some do not: `focus` and `blur` (use `focusin` and `focusout`, which do), `mouseenter` and `mouseleave`, and `load` or `error` on an ``. `stopPropagation()` stops the journey at the current element; `stopImmediatePropagation()` also skips the remaining listeners on that same element. Neither cancels the default action; that is `preventDefault()`'s job.

Click the button in the widget and read the log. Then tick `stopPropagation()` and see `body` and `document` never hear about the click. Tick **delegate** and click the list items: one listener on the `ul` handles all three.
Event delegation

Because clicks bubble, you do not need a listener on every row. Put **one** listener on a stable container and ask, inside it, which item the click came from with `e.target.closest(...)`. This uses less memory, needs no clean-up when rows are removed, and, most importantly, works for rows that **do not exist yet** when the listener is attached.

Fires when
Bubbles
Notes

A classic `<script src="app.js">` in `<head>` runs as soon as the parser reaches it, **before** `<body>` is parsed, so `document.querySelector('#status')` returns `null` and the next line throws `TypeError: Cannot set properties of null`. Runs when
Order
rows: after parsing (modules are deferred by default)
when the parser reaches it (elements above exist)
as soon as it downloads, maybe before parsing ends
**any** order: only for independent scripts such as analytics

blocks.name: element.addEventListener()
blocks.sum: Register a function to be called whenever an event of the given type reaches the element.
blocks.syntax: target.addEventListener(type, listener, { once, capture, passive, signal } | useCapture)

how.text: Adds `listener` to the target's list for `type`. When an event of that type is dispatched and its path passes through the target in the matching phase (bubble by default, capture with `capture: true`), the browser calls the listener with the event object; `this` inside a `function` listener is `e.currentTarget` (arrow functions keep the outer `this`). Several listeners can share a type and run in registration order. Adding the very same function twice for the same type and phase is ignored.
The older `el.onclick = fn` property holds exactly one handler and a second assignment silently replaces the first. Prefer `addEventListener`.

blocks.sum: Unregister a listener previously added with the same type, function and capture flag.

how.text: The browser finds the listener by the triple (type, function object, capture flag). It must be the **same function object**, so an inline arrow function can never be removed: the arrow you pass to `removeEventListener` is a new function. Keep a named reference, or use the `signal` option and an `AbortController`, which removes any number of listeners with one `abort()` call.

blocks.name: event.target
blocks.sum: The element where the event started; currentTarget is the element whose listener is running.

how.text: When you click the `<b>` inside an `<li>` inside a `<ul>` that has the listener, `e.target` is the `<b>` and `e.currentTarget` is the `<ul>`. `target` stays the same for the whole journey; `currentTarget` changes at each stop and is `null` once dispatch is over (so read it synchronously, not after an `await`).
For delegation, start at `target` and climb with `closest()` to the item you care about.

blocks.name: event.preventDefault()
blocks.sum: Cancel the browser's default action for this event, such as following a link or submitting a form.

how.text: Many events have a built-in consequence that runs after all listeners: a `submit` navigates to the form's `action`, a click on a link follows `href`, a `keydown` types a character, a checkbox click toggles it. Calling `preventDefault()` in any listener during dispatch cancels that consequence (if the event is cancelable). `defaultPrevented` tells later listeners that someone already did.
It does **not** stop propagation; other listeners still run.

blocks.name: event.stopPropagation()
blocks.sum: Stop the event from reaching any further elements on its capture or bubble path.

how.text: Dispatch continues to the remaining listeners on the current element, then stops: ancestors (bubbling) or descendants (capturing) never see the event. `stopImmediatePropagation()` also skips the remaining listeners on the current element. Use it sparingly: a click that never reaches `document` breaks every "close the menu when you click elsewhere" handler.

blocks.name: element.dispatchEvent()
blocks.sum: Fire an event at an element yourself, including CustomEvent objects that carry your own data.
blocks.syntax: target.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(type, { detail, bubbles, cancelable })) -> boolean

how.text: Runs the full capture, target and bubble path **synchronously**: every listener has finished before `dispatchEvent` returns. It returns `false` if a listener called `preventDefault()` on a cancelable event. Events you create default to `bubbles: false`, so pass `bubbles: true` when ancestors should hear them. `isTrusted` is `false` for these. A `CustomEvent` with a namespaced type (`device:selected`) and a `detail` payload lets one part of a page announce something without knowing who listens.

blocks.text: Forms, FormData and validation

A form submission is an event like any other. Listen for `submit` on the **form** (it fires for button clicks and for Enter in a text field), call `preventDefault()`, read the fields with `FormData`, and send them with `fetch`. You keep the browser's free features: Enter to submit, autofill, password managers, and built-in validation.

`new FormData(form)` collects exactly what a real submission would send: each successful control with a `name`. Unchecked checkboxes, disabled fields and fields without a `name` are left out, and every value is a string (`'on'` for a checked box without a `value`).

blocks.text: The constraint validation API is what the browser uses for `required`, `type="email"`, `pattern`, `min`/`max` and `maxlength`:

items.text: `el.validity` is a `ValidityState` with one flag per rule (`valueMissing`, `typeMismatch`, `patternMismatch`, `rangeOverflow`, `tooLong`, `customError`) and a summary `valid`.
`form.checkValidity()` and `el.checkValidity()` return a boolean and fire `invalid` events; `reportValidity()` also shows the browser's message bubbles.

`el.setCustomValidity(msg)` marks a field invalid with your own message, for rules HTML cannot express (octets above 255, a name that is already taken). **Reset it with `''`** or the field stays invalid forever.

`form.requestSubmit()` behaves like clicking a submit button: validation runs first, and `submit` fires only if everything passes. The older `form.submit()` skips both validation and the `submit` event, so your listener never runs.

A `novalidate` attribute on the form switches the browser's checks off at submit time so your code (or the server) reports errors; the CSS pseudo-classes `:invalid` and `:user-invalid` (only after the user has interacted) still work for styling.

blocks.text: The server must validate anyway: anyone can send a request with `curl` and skip your page entirely. The practice API does, and it answers with `400` or `422` and a JSON error. Use this playground and its **Network** pane:

Passed directly as a `fetch` body, it is sent as `multipart/form-data` with a generated boundary, which is what file uploads need. Wrap it as `new URLSearchParams(fd)` for `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, or convert to an object and `JSON.stringify` it for a JSON API.

blocks.text: Rendering lists from data

Most interactive pages follow one loop: **fetch data, turn it into elements, put them on the page, react to events, repeat.** Write the "turn into elements" part as a function of the data (`render(devices)`), and always handle three states besides success: **loading**, **empty** and **error**. A list that silently stays blank when the API returns `500` is the most common front-end bug report.

blocks.out:
/api/error -> Could not load devices (HTTP 500). 0
/api/devices?type=camera -> No devices match. 0
/api/devices -> 6 devices 6
nas

blocks.text: `fetch` only rejects on network failure; an HTTP `500` is a successful *response*, which is why the code checks `res.ok` (status 200-299) and throws itself. Details of `fetch`, `res.ok` and `AbortController` are in [JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper).
Re-render or update?

`replaceChildren(fragment)` throws away the old rows and builds new ones. It is simple and correct, and for a few hundred rows it is fast. It also destroys state the user cares about: focus inside a row, a half-typed edit, the scroll position of a nested box, a CSS transition in progress. When that matters, **update in place**: keep a `Map` from id to element, change only the rows whose data changed, add new ids, remove missing ones. Frameworks like React and Vue automate exactly this "keyed diff"; doing it by hand once teaches you what they do.
Timers in the UI: polling and debouncing

**Polling** means asking the server again on a schedule (`/api/status` every 5 seconds) and showing when you last succeeded. Prefer a `setTimeout` chain, which schedules the next request only after the previous one finished, to `setInterval`, which fires on schedule even if a slow response is still pending and can stack requests on a bad network. Stop polling when the tab is hidden (`document.visibilityState === 'hidden'`, `visibilitychange` event) to save battery and server load.

**Debouncing** means waiting until the user stops typing before acting. Without it, typing `printer` into a search box fires seven requests and the responses can arrive out of order, so the list may end up showing results for `pri`. A debounce restarts a timer on every call and only runs the function when the timer survives:

blocks.out:
search for nas
search for printer

blocks.text: Three calls at 0 ms and one at 50 ms all landed inside the 200 ms quiet window, so only the last (`nas`) ran, at 250 ms. The call at 600 ms came after a pause and ran too. This block is plain JavaScript with no DOM, so it runs the same in Node. The closure over `timer` is what makes it work ([closures](#js-deeper)). Pair a debounce with an `AbortController` so that a response for an old query can never overwrite a newer one.

blocks.text: Remembering state with localStorage

`localStorage` is a small, synchronous key/value store per **origin** (scheme + host + port), shared by every tab of that origin and kept across restarts. `sessionStorage` has the same API but lives only as long as the tab. Both store **strings only**: anything else is converted with `String()`, so objects must go through `JSON.stringify` and come back with `JSON.parse`.

blocks.text: What it is good for: UI preferences such as a theme, a saved filter, a collapsed panel, an unsent draft. What it is not for: anything secret. Every script on the origin can read it, so one XSS bug leaks every token stored there; an `HttpOnly` cookie set by the server is out of script's reach. Quotas are roughly 5 MB per origin in current browsers (hedged: browsers differ), `setItem` throws `QuotaExceededError` when full, and private-browsing modes or blocked site data can make it throw or start empty, so wrap access in `try`/`catch` and keep the page working without it. A `storage` event fires in the *other* tabs of the origin when one tab changes a value.

blocks.text: Performance: batching, layout and observers

To draw a frame the engine runs a pipeline: compute **style** for the elements that changed, compute **layout** (sizes and positions), **paint** pixels, then **composite** layers. DOM writes do not run that pipeline immediately; they mark things dirty, and the work happens once before the next frame. A *read* of a layout value (`offsetWidth`, `offsetTop`, `getBoundingClientRect()`, `scrollHeight`, `getComputedStyle().width`, `innerText`) forces the engine to bring layout up to date **now** so it can answer. Alternate writes and reads in a loop and you force a full layout per iteration: **layout thrashing**.

⟪r:thrashing⟫  write ▸ ⟪r:READ⟫ ▸ layout ▸ write ▸ ⟪r:READ⟫ ▸ layout ▸ write ▸ ⟪r:READ⟫ ▸ layout ...   N layouts
 ⟪g:batched⟫    ⟪g:READ READ READ ...⟫ ▸ (1 layout) ▸ write write write ... ▸ next frame: 1 layout     2 layouts
               └──────── JavaScript task ────────┘        └─ style ▸ layout ▸ paint ▸ composite ─┘

blocks.text: Rules that keep pages fast:

items.text: **Read first, then write.** Gather every measurement you need, then apply every change.
**Batch insertions** with a `DocumentFragment`, `append(...nodes)` or `replaceChildren`.
**Toggle a class** instead of setting five inline properties; CSS does the rest in one style pass.
**Animate with `transform` and `opacity`**, which the compositor can move without layout; and schedule visual work with `requestAnimationFrame`.
**Delegate** events instead of attaching thousands of listeners.

Watching the DOM: MutationObserver

A `MutationObserver` calls you back when nodes are added or removed, attributes change, or text changes, inside a subtree you choose. Callbacks are **batched and asynchronous**: the browser collects the records and delivers them as a microtask after the current script finishes, so a loop that adds 100 nodes produces one callback, not 100.

Seeing what is visible: IntersectionObserver

An `IntersectionObserver` tells you when an element enters or leaves the viewport (or a scrolling container), computed by the browser during its rendering steps, without scroll listeners or layout reads in your code. It powers lazy loading, "load more" lists and "mark as read".

blocks.name: new MutationObserver()
blocks.sum: Get batched, asynchronous callbacks when nodes, attributes or text change inside an observed subtree.
blocks.syntax: const mo = new MutationObserver((records, observer) => {...}); mo.observe(target, { childList, attributes, characterData, subtree, attributeFilter, attributeOldValue }); mo.disconnect(); mo.takeRecords()

how.text: You choose what to watch with the options object: `childList` (children added or removed), `attributes` (optionally limited by `attributeFilter`), `characterData` (text changes), and `subtree` to include all descendants. Each `MutationRecord` has `type`, `target`, `addedNodes`, `removedNodes`, `attributeName` and, if requested, `oldValue`.

Records are queued and delivered as a **microtask** after the current script, so the callback sees the final state of a burst of changes. `disconnect()` stops observing; `takeRecords()` empties the queue synchronously.

blocks.name: new IntersectionObserver()
blocks.sum: Get a callback when observed elements start or stop intersecting the viewport or a scroll container.
blocks.syntax: const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {...}, { root, rootMargin, threshold }); io.observe(el); io.unobserve(el); io.disconnect()

how.text: The browser computes intersections during its rendering steps, off your JavaScript, and calls back with `IntersectionObserverEntry` objects (`target`, `isIntersecting`, `intersectionRatio`, `boundingClientRect`). `root` is the scrolling ancestor (default: the viewport), `rootMargin` grows or shrinks it like CSS margins (start loading 200 px early), and `threshold` lists the visible fractions that trigger callbacks (`[0, 0.5, 1]`). It replaces scroll listeners that call `getBoundingClientRect()` on every frame.

blocks.name: requestAnimationFrame()
blocks.sum: Run a function right before the browser's next repaint, once.

how.text: The callback runs in the rendering step of the event loop, just before style, layout and paint, usually 60 times a second (more on ProMotion displays) and **not at all** in background tabs. That makes it the right place for visual updates driven by JavaScript: you do your writes once per frame, aligned with the display, instead of whenever a timer or message happens to fire. The `timestamp` argument lets you animate by elapsed time instead of by frame count. For a continuous animation, call it again from inside the callback.

examples.desc: Coalesce many updates into one write per frame
examples.code: let queued = false; function schedule() { if (!queued) { queued = true; requestAnimationFrame(() => { queued = false; draw(); }); } }

examples.desc: Animate a meter towards a target value over time

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **The script runs before the element exists.** `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'addEventListener')` in Chrome (Safari: `null is not an object`, Firefox: `btn is null`). Add `defer` or `type="module"`, or move the script to the end of `<body>`.
**Treating a NodeList as an array.** `querySelectorAll(...).map is not a function`. Use `[...list]` or `Array.from(list)`.
**Attaching listeners to elements that do not exist yet.** Rows rendered after the `forEach` have no listener. Delegate to the container.
**`innerHTML +=` in a loop.** Re-parses the whole container each time, drops listeners and form state, and is an XSS sink. Build nodes, append once.
**Forgetting `preventDefault()` on submit.** The page reloads and your `fetch` is cancelled mid-flight; in DevTools the request shows as "(canceled)".
**`dataset` and form values are strings.** `'false'` is truthy, `'8080' + 1` is `'80801'`. Use `input.valueAsNumber` for number inputs and compare strings explicitly.

blocks.title: Write debounce

task.text: Implement `debounce(fn, ms)`. It returns a function that, when called repeatedly, waits until `ms` milliseconds pass **without** another call and then calls `fn` once with the **latest** arguments. Give the returned function a `cancel()` method that drops a pending call. The check calls it with timers, so print nothing.

hints: `let timer;` in `debounce`, then inside the returned function `clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);`.

why.text: Each call clears the previous timer, so only the last one in a burst survives the quiet period, and because the arrow function captures `args` from that last call, `fn` sees the latest input. Functions are objects in JavaScript, so hanging `cancel` on the returned function is ordinary property assignment.
